claim: Single cell isolation from helminth-infected murine intestines has been notoriously difficult due to strong anti-parasite type 2 immune responses that drive mucus production, tissue remodeling and immune cell infiltration.
source: Single cell isolation from helminth-infected murine intestines has been notoriously difficult, due to the strong anti-parasite type 2 immune responses that drive mucus production, tissue remodeling and immune cell infiltration.
evidence: This is stated as a known challenge in the field, supported by the context of the study and references to tissue changes during infection.

claim: The optimized cell isolation protocol successfully isolates millions of immune cells from heavily infected duodenum.
source: Through the systematic optimization of a standard intestinal digestion protocol, we were able to successfully isolate millions of immune cells from the heavily infected duodenum.
evidence: The abstract states this as a primary finding, supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The cell isolation protocol and high-dimensional analysis identified many known hallmarks of anti-parasite immune responses throughout the entire course of helminth infection.
source: Our cell isolation protocol and high-dimensional analysis allowed us to identify many known hallmarks of anti-parasite immune responses throughout the entire course of helminth infection and has the potential to accelerate single-cell discoveries of local helminth immune responses that have previously been unfeasible.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by spectral flow cytometry data and confocal microscopy validation throughout the manuscript.

claim: Recent advances in single cell analysis have significantly increased understanding of multiple diseases and cell types in different tissues.
source: Recent advances in single cell analysis have significantly increased our understanding of multiple diseases and cell types in different tissues (Svensson et al., 2018; Hwang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Many single cell technologies require single cell suspensions as input, which limits assessment of difficult-to-process tissues.
source: However, many of these technologies require single cell suspensions as an input, which limits our assessment of difficult-to-process tissues (Hwang et al., 2018; Nguyen et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature discussing technical limitations.

claim: The intestine is at the center of many research questions focusing on nutrient uptake, host-microbiome interactions, local and systemic immune tolerance, and gastrointestinal diseases and infections.
source: One prominent example is the intestine, which is at the center of many research questions that focus on nutrient uptake (Kiela and Ghishan, 2016), host-microbiome interactions (Belkaid and Hand, 2014; Tilg et al., 2019; Sekirov et al., 2010), local and systemic immune tolerance (Worbs et al., 2006; Harrison and Powrie, 2013; Whibley et al., 2019) and gastrointestinal diseases and infections (Mowat and Agace, 2014; Sell and Dolan, 2018; Fletcher et al., 2013; Hendrickson et al., 2002; Saleh and Elson, 2011), but represents a challenging tissue to digest (Weigmann et al., 2007; Reißig et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research in these areas.

claim: The intestine represents a challenging tissue to digest.
source: One prominent example is the intestine, which is at the center of many research questions that focus on nutrient uptake (Kiela and Ghishan, 2016), host-microbiome interactions (Belkaid and Hand, 2014; Tilg et al., 2019; Sekirov et al., 2010), local and systemic immune tolerance (Worbs et al., 2006; Harrison and Powrie, 2013; Whibley et al., 2019) and gastrointestinal diseases and infections (Mowat and Agace, 2014; Sell and Dolan, 2018; Fletcher et al., 2013; Hendrickson et al., 2002; Saleh and Elson, 2011), but represents a challenging tissue to digest (Weigmann et al., 2007; Reißig et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published protocols and the context of the study.

claim: The standard digestion procedure to isolate intestinal immune cells from small intestinal lamina propria consists of three steps: collection and preparation, EDTA wash steps, and enzymatic digestion.
source: The standard digestion procedure to isolate intestinal immune cells located in the small intestinal lamina propria consists of three steps (Weigmann et al., 2007; Reißig et al., 2014; Scott et al., 2016; Esterházy et al., 2019) (Figure 1a). First the intestinal segment of interest is collected, opened longitudinally to remove its luminal content, washed and cut into small pieces. These pieces then undergo several wash steps with EDTA containing wash buffers at 37°C to remove the epithelial layer and make the lamina propria accessible for enzymatic digestion. Lastly, the tissue is enzymatically digested with collagenases (Collagenase VIII from Clostridium histolyticum being among the most popular) and later filtered to obtain a single cell suspension.
evidence: This is described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1a, with citations to established protocols.

claim: Collagenase VIII from Clostridium histolyticum is among the most popular enzymes for intestinal digestion.
source: Lastly, the tissue is enzymatically digested with collagenases (Collagenase VIII from Clostridium histolyticum being among the most popular) and later filtered to obtain a single cell suspension.
evidence: This is stated as common practice in the field, supported by citations to standard protocols.

claim: The standard digestion method results in high cell yield from steady state intestines but isolation of cells from severely infected segments remains challenging.
source: While this method results in a high cell yield from steady state intestines, the isolation of cells from severely infected segments remains challenging (Reißig et al., 2014; Scott et al., 2016; Webster et al., 2020) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by citations and demonstrated in Figure 1b showing poor cell recovery from infected samples using standard protocol.

claim: Intestinal helminths represent over 50% of all parasitic infections in human and livestock populations.
source: One of the most prominent examples are infections with intestinal helminths, which represent over 50% of all parasitic infections in human and livestock populations (McSorley and Maizels, 2012; Hotez et al., 2008; Jourdan et al., 2018; Jackson et al., 2009).
evidence: This statistic is supported by multiple citations to epidemiological literature.

claim: Limited cell isolation from infected intestines has restricted analysis of anti-parasite immune responses to imaging approaches, phenotypical observations in transgenic mouse strains, or assessment of secondary locations.
source: This has limited our analysis of anti-parasite immune responses to imaging approaches, phenotypical observations in transgenic mouse strains or the assessment of secondary locations like the draining lymph nodes, blood or spleen (McSorley and Maizels, 2012; Maizels and McSorley, 2016; Mishra et al., 2014), which might only partially reflect local immunity.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of technical limitations, supported by citations to studies using these alternative approaches.

claim: Secondary locations like draining lymph nodes, blood, or spleen might only partially reflect local immunity during helminth infection.
source: This has limited our analysis of anti-parasite immune responses to imaging approaches, phenotypical observations in transgenic mouse strains or the assessment of secondary locations like the draining lymph nodes, blood or spleen (McSorley and Maizels, 2012; Maizels and McSorley, 2016; Mishra et al., 2014), which might only partially reflect local immunity.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation and later supported by data showing differences between lamina propria and draining lymph nodes.

claim: Helminth infections are strongly linked to chronic impairments affecting nutrition availability.
source: As helminth infections are strongly linked to chronic impairments that affect nutrition availability (Koski and Scott, 2001; Crompton and Nesheim, 2002); memory, cognition and physical development (Ezeamama et al., 2005; Pabalan et al., 2018; Nokes et al., 1992); changes in the microbiota (Gause and Maizels, 2016; Ramanan et al., 2016) and modulation of local and systemic immunity (Mishra et al., 2014; Maizels et al., 2009), an optimized digestion protocol is needed to further investigate the infected intestinal tissue.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on helminth-associated pathology.

claim: Helminth infections are strongly linked to chronic impairments affecting memory, cognition and physical development.
source: As helminth infections are strongly linked to chronic impairments that affect nutrition availability (Koski and Scott, 2001; Crompton and Nesheim, 2002); memory, cognition and physical development (Ezeamama et al., 2005; Pabalan et al., 2018; Nokes et al., 1992); changes in the microbiota (Gause and Maizels, 2016; Ramanan et al., 2016) and modulation of local and systemic immunity (Mishra et al., 2014; Maizels et al., 2009), an optimized digestion protocol is needed to further investigate the infected intestinal tissue.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on helminth-associated pathology.

source: As helminth infections are strongly linked to chronic impairments that affect nutrition availability (Koski and Scott, 2001; Crompton and Nesheim, 2002); memory, cognition and physical development (Ezeamama et al., 2005; Pabalan et al., 2018; Nokes et al., 1992); changes in the microbiota (Gause and Maizels, 2016; Ramanan et al., 2016) and modulation of local and systemic immunity (Mishra et al., 2014; Maizels et al., 2009), an optimized digestion protocol is needed to further investigate the infected intestinal tissue.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on helminth-microbiota interactions.

claim: Helminth infections are strongly linked to modulation of local and systemic immunity.
source: As helminth infections are strongly linked to chronic impairments that affect nutrition availability (Koski and Scott, 2001; Crompton and Nesheim, 2002); memory, cognition and physical development (Ezeamama et al., 2005; Pabalan et al., 2018; Nokes et al., 1992); changes in the microbiota (Gause and Maizels, 2016; Ramanan et al., 2016) and modulation of local and systemic immunity (Mishra et al., 2014; Maizels et al., 2009), an optimized digestion protocol is needed to further investigate the infected intestinal tissue.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on helminth immunomodulation.

claim: Difficulties with intestinal digests during helminth infection have been associated with strong anti-parasite type 2 immune response that drives mucus production.
source: Difficulties with intestinal digests during helminth infection have been associated with a strong anti-parasite type 2 immune response that drives mucus production (Hashimoto et al., 2009; von Moltke et al., 2016), alters the epithelium (Gerbe et al., 2016; Howitt et al., 2016), induces immune cell infiltration (Inclan-Rico and Siracusa, 2018) and causes tissue remodelling (Motran et al., 2018; Boyett and Hsieh, 2014) (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by citations and demonstrated in Figure 1c showing tissue changes.

claim: Strong anti-parasite type 2 immune response alters the epithelium during helminth infection.
source: Difficulties with intestinal digests during helminth infection have been associated with a strong anti-parasite type 2 immune response that drives mucus production (Hashimoto et al., 2009; von Moltke et al., 2016), alters the epithelium (Gerbe et al., 2016; Howitt et al., 2016), induces immune cell infiltration (Inclan-Rico and Siracusa, 2018) and causes tissue remodelling (Motran et al., 2018; Boyett and Hsieh, 2014) (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by citations and demonstrated in Figure 1c.

claim: Strong anti-parasite type 2 immune response induces immune cell infiltration during helminth infection.
source: Difficulties with intestinal digests during helminth infection have been associated with a strong anti-parasite type 2 immune response that drives mucus production (Hashimoto et al., 2009; von Moltke et al., 2016), alters the epithelium (Gerbe et al., 2016; Howitt et al., 2016), induces immune cell infiltration (Inclan-Rico and Siracusa, 2018) and causes tissue remodelling (Motran et al., 2018; Boyett and Hsieh, 2014) (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by citations and demonstrated in Figure 1c showing increased CD45+ cells.

claim: Strong anti-parasite type 2 immune response causes tissue remodelling during helminth infection.
source: Difficulties with intestinal digests during helminth infection have been associated with a strong anti-parasite type 2 immune response that drives mucus production (Hashimoto et al., 2009; von Moltke et al., 2016), alters the epithelium (Gerbe et al., 2016; Howitt et al., 2016), induces immune cell infiltration (Inclan-Rico and Siracusa, 2018) and causes tissue remodelling (Motran et al., 2018; Boyett and Hsieh, 2014) (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by citations and demonstrated in Figure 1c.

claim: C57BL/6 mice were infected with Heligmosomoides polygyrus bakeri to investigate a model of both acute and chronic helminth infection.
source: In order to investigate a model of both acute and chronic helminth infection, we infected C57BL/6 mice with Heligmosomoides polygyrus bakeri (also known as Heligmosomoides bakeri; Behnke and Harris, 2010), a naturally occurring rodent parasite with an exclusive intestinal life cycle (Monroy and Enriquez, 1992; Reynolds et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the experimental model used, supported by citations about the parasite.

claim: Heligmosomoides polygyrus bakeri is a naturally occurring rodent parasite with an exclusive intestinal life cycle.
source: In order to investigate a model of both acute and chronic helminth infection, we infected C57BL/6 mice with Heligmosomoides polygyrus bakeri (also known as Heligmosomoides bakeri; Behnke and Harris, 2010), a naturally occurring rodent parasite with an exclusive intestinal life cycle (Monroy and Enriquez, 1992; Reynolds et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on the parasite biology.

claim: Infective L3 larvae of H. polygyrus penetrate the intestinal tissue of the duodenum within 24 hr of ingestion.
source: Infective L3 larvae penetrate the intestinal tissue of the duodenum within 24 hr of ingestion, undergo larval development in the muscularis externa and return to the lumen within 10 days post infection, where the adult worms mate and develop a chronic infection in C57BL/6 mice (Reynolds et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the parasite life cycle, supported by citations.

claim: H. polygyrus larvae undergo larval development in the muscularis externa.
source: Infective L3 larvae penetrate the intestinal tissue of the duodenum within 24 hr of ingestion, undergo larval development in the muscularis externa and return to the lumen within 10 days post infection, where the adult worms mate and develop a chronic infection in C57BL/6 mice (Reynolds et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the parasite life cycle, supported by citations.

claim: H. polygyrus larvae return to the lumen within 10 days post infection.
source: Infective L3 larvae penetrate the intestinal tissue of the duodenum within 24 hr of ingestion, undergo larval development in the muscularis externa and return to the lumen within 10 days post infection, where the adult worms mate and develop a chronic infection in C57BL/6 mice (Reynolds et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the parasite life cycle, supported by citations.

claim: Adult H. polygyrus worms mate and develop a chronic infection in C57BL/6 mice.
source: Infective L3 larvae penetrate the intestinal tissue of the duodenum within 24 hr of ingestion, undergo larval development in the muscularis externa and return to the lumen within 10 days post infection, where the adult worms mate and develop a chronic infection in C57BL/6 mice (Reynolds et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the parasite life cycle in this mouse strain, supported by citations.

claim: The peak of acute immunity during H. polygyrus infection is usually studied around day 14 post infection.
source: The peak of acute immunity is usually studied around day 14 post infection and we focused on this time point and the heavily infected duodenum (Filbey et al., 2014; Elliott et al., 2008), to optimize our digestion protocol.
evidence: This is stated as established practice in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Modifying the EDTA wash steps to remove increased mucus did not improve cell yield from infected intestines.
source: First, we modified the EDTA wash steps to remove the increased amount of mucus but did not observe an improvement in cell yield (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; digestion protocols #1, 2, 6).
evidence: This is stated as a result of systematic testing, shown in Figure 1d and supplement.

claim: Collagenase A from Clostridium histolyticum showed an increase in cell yield when used with the standard digestion protocol for infected intestines.
source: Indeed, we found that Collagenase A from Clostridium histolyticum (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; digestion protocols #7, 8), but not Collagenase VIII, Collagenase D, Dispase or Liberase TM (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; digestion protocols #3–5), showed an increase in cell yield when used in conjunction with the standard digestion protocol.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1d and supplement.

claim: Collagenase VIII, Collagenase D, Dispase and Liberase TM did not show an increase in cell yield when used with the standard digestion protocol for infected intestines.
source: Indeed, we found that Collagenase A from Clostridium histolyticum (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; digestion protocols #7, 8), but not Collagenase VIII, Collagenase D, Dispase or Liberase TM (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; digestion protocols #3–5), showed an increase in cell yield when used in conjunction with the standard digestion protocol.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1d and supplement.

claim: Strong vortexing after each wash step significantly improved the outcome of digestion for infected intestines.
source: Importantly, strong vortexing after each wash step significantly improved the outcome of digestion (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 2; digestion protocol #13), suggesting that the epithelium is harder to remove in helminth-infected tissues.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1d and supplement.

claim: The epithelium is harder to remove in helminth-infected tissues.
source: Importantly, strong vortexing after each wash step significantly improved the outcome of digestion (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 2; digestion protocol #13), suggesting that the epithelium is harder to remove in helminth-infected tissues.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that vortexing improved digestion outcomes.

claim: Physiological changes that impair intestinal digest using the standard protocol are linked to type two immune responses.
source: Indeed, observations from Stat6ko mice confirmed that the physiological changes that impair the intestinal digest using the standard protocol, were all linked to type two immune responses, as intestines from infected Stat6ko mice could readily be digested (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing digestion outcomes in Stat6ko mice (which lack type 2 responses) versus wild-type mice.

claim: Intestines from infected Stat6ko mice could readily be digested using the standard protocol.
source: Indeed, observations from Stat6ko mice confirmed that the physiological changes that impair the intestinal digest using the standard protocol, were all linked to type two immune responses, as intestines from infected Stat6ko mice could readily be digested (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: No CD45+ cells were detected in the EDTA wash from infected animals.
source: We also assessed intra-epithelial cells in the EDTA wash, but could not detect any CD45+ cells in preparations from infected animals, emphasizing that our protocol should only be used to isolate lamina propria cells.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: The optimized protocol should only be used to isolate lamina propria cells, not intra-epithelial cells.
source: We also assessed intra-epithelial cells in the EDTA wash, but could not detect any CD45+ cells in preparations from infected animals, emphasizing that our protocol should only be used to isolate lamina propria cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that no intra-epithelial cells were recovered.

claim: Gradient centrifugation resulted in a dramatic drop in cell yield and was therefore omitted from the optimized protocol.
source: Several intestinal cell isolation protocols also utilize a final gradient centrifugation step to further isolate immune cells (Weigmann et al., 2007; Esterházy et al., 2019). However, in our hands this resulted in a dramatic drop in cell yield and was therefore omitted (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 2; digestion protocol #14).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1d and supplement.

claim: The optimized lamina propria cell isolation protocol includes three 10 min 2 mM EDTA wash steps each followed by vigorous vortexing and a 30 min digest with 1 mg/ml Collagenase A, 20% FCS and 0.05 mg/ml DNase.
source: Our optimized lamina propria cell isolation protocol for H. polygyrus-infected intestines thus included three 10 min 2 mM EDTA wash steps (each followed by vigorous vortexing) and a 30 min digest with 1 mg/ml Collagenase A, 20% FCS and 0.05 mg/ml DNase (see Appendix 1 for step-by-step instructions).
evidence: This describes the final optimized protocol developed through systematic testing.

claim: Intestinal digests from naïve animals using the standard or optimized cell isolation protocol showed highly comparable outcomes.
source: When we compared intestinal digests from naïve animals using the standard or optimized cell isolation protocol, we observed highly comparable outcomes (Figure 1d; digestion protocols #1 and 13).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Both standard and optimized digestion protocols resulted in a cell yield of 3–6 million live cells per duodenum with 70–80% viability and 20–30% frequency of CD45+ cells from naïve animals.
source: Both digestion protocols resulted in a cell yield of 3–6 million live cells per duodenum with 70–80% viability and 20–30% frequency of CD45+ cells.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result comparing the two protocols on naïve samples.

claim: Samples from all time points of H. polygyrus infection (day 7, 14, and 28) could be successfully digested using the optimized digestion protocol.
source: We observed that samples from all time points could be successfully digested using our optimized digestion protocol and that duodenal digests from 14- and 28 days post infection yielded 3–6 million live cells per sample (Figure 1e,f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1e,f.

claim: Duodenal digests from 14 and 28 days post H. polygyrus infection yielded 3–6 million live cells per sample.
source: We observed that samples from all time points could be successfully digested using our optimized digestion protocol and that duodenal digests from 14- and 28 days post infection yielded 3–6 million live cells per sample (Figure 1e,f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: A consistent doubling of cell count to 8–11 million live cells per duodenum was observed at day 7 post H. polygyrus infection.
source: We furthermore observed a consistent doubling of the cell count to 8–11 million live cells per duodenum at day seven post infection and observed a similar trend when we quantified CD45+ cells in cryosections from these time points (Figure 1f,g).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1f,g.

claim: A similar trend of increased cell numbers at day 7 was observed when CD45+ cells were quantified in cryosections.
source: We furthermore observed a consistent doubling of the cell count to 8–11 million live cells per duodenum at day seven post infection and observed a similar trend when we quantified CD45+ cells in cryosections from these time points (Figure 1f,g).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: A 23-color spectral flow cytometry panel was used to characterize isolated cells and incorporated hallmark surface and intracellular markers for type two immune responses associated with helminth infections.
source: To understand these differences and validate whether our protocol was suitable for subsequent single cell analysis and immunophenotyping, we characterized the isolated cells further using a 23-color spectral flow cytometry panel that incorporated many of the hallmark surface and intracellular markers for type two immune responses that have been associated with helminth infections (Maizels and McSorley, 2016; Reynolds et al., 2012) (see Supplementary file 1 for details regarding markers, fluorophores, clones and staining concentrations used).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used, with citations supporting the marker selection.

claim: The staining panel was designed to identify both innate and adaptive immune cell populations including eosinophils, neutrophils, monocyte subsets, macrophages, dendritic cells, ILC subsets, T helper subsets, T regulatory cells, and B cells.
source: Our staining panel was designed to identify both innate and adaptive immune cell populations and allowed us to assess eosinophils, neutrophils, different subsets of monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells, as well as the three main populations of innate lymphoid cells (ILC1, ILC2, and ILC3) and effector T cells populations (Th1, Th2, Th17), T regulatory cells and B cells as well as their proliferation through ki67 expression within the same panel.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the flow cytometry panel developed.

claim: Collagenase digestion can negatively affect surface epitope integrity.
source: To guarantee optimal staining conditions, we tested our optimized digestion protocol on splenocytes and compared digested to non-digested cells, as collagenase digests can negatively affect surface epitope integrity.
evidence: This is stated as a known concern that motivated the validation experiment.

claim: A reduction in MFIs of Ly6G, MHCII, CD45 and CD127 was observed after collagenase digestion, but all positive stained cell populations could be clearly identified.
source: While we observed a reduction in the MFIs of several markers (namely Ly6G, MHCII, CD45 and CD127), all positive stained cell populations could be clearly identified (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Different commercial intracellular staining kits significantly affected cellular scatter profiles and varied in the resolution of intracellular antibody staining.
source: Isolated intestinal lamina propria cells also proved a challenge for intracellular staining, as different commercial intracellular staining kits significantly affected the cellular, but not debris, scatter profiles and varied in the resolution of intracellularly antibody staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The eBioscience FoxP3/Transcription Factor Staining Buffer Set yielded the best results for intracellular staining of intestinal lamina propria cells.
source: In our hands, the eBioscience FoxP3/Transcription Factor Staining Buffer Set yielded the best results and was used henceforth.
evidence: This is stated as the result of comparing different commercial kits shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: A strong infiltration of immune cells such as neutrophils and monocytes was observed at day 7 post H. polygyrus infection.
source: In line with previous findings (Inclan-Rico and Siracusa, 2018), we observed a strong infiltration of immune cells such as neutrophils and monocytes at day 7 post infection, which we verified by confocal microscopy and were primarily localized around the developing larvae explaining the increase in total cell number at this timepoint (Figure 2a–c and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry and confocal microscopy data, and supported by citation.

claim: Infiltrating immune cells at day 7 post infection were primarily localized around the developing larvae.
source: In line with previous findings (Inclan-Rico and Siracusa, 2018), we observed a strong infiltration of immune cells such as neutrophils and monocytes at day 7 post infection, which we verified by confocal microscopy and were primarily localized around the developing larvae explaining the increase in total cell number at this timepoint (Figure 2a–c and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2c and supplement 3.

claim: The localization of infiltrating immune cells around developing larvae explains the increase in total cell number at day 7 post infection.
source: In line with previous findings (Inclan-Rico and Siracusa, 2018), we observed a strong infiltration of immune cells such as neutrophils and monocytes at day 7 post infection, which we verified by confocal microscopy and were primarily localized around the developing larvae explaining the increase in total cell number at this timepoint (Figure 2a–c and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial localization data and cell count data.

claim: The inflammatory response receded at later time points after day 7, which was likely linked to the worms exiting the intestinal tissue and inhabiting the lumen.
source: At later time points this inflammatory response receded, which was likely linked to the worms exiting the intestinal tissue and inhabiting the lumen.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing decreased inflammation at later timepoints and knowledge of the parasite life cycle.

claim: Peak expression of RELMα in resident macrophages was observed at day 14 post infection and was localized within the granulomas.
source: Peak expression of RELMα in resident macrophages, which is a hallmark for their alternative activation and wound repair responses (Esser-von Bieren et al., 2013; Krljanac et al., 2019), was observed at day 14 and was again localized within the granulomas (Figure 2b,c and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry and confocal microscopy data, supported by citations.

claim: RELMα expression is a hallmark for alternative activation and wound repair responses in macrophages.
source: Peak expression of RELMα in resident macrophages, which is a hallmark for their alternative activation and wound repair responses (Esser-von Bieren et al., 2013; Krljanac et al., 2019), was observed at day 14 and was again localized within the granulomas (Figure 2b,c and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Type two innate lymphoid cells did not increase in frequency over time during H. polygyrus infection, but ki67 expression increased suggesting cell proliferation and activation.
source: While type two innate lymphoid cells did not increase in frequency over time, ki67 expression increased, suggesting cell proliferation and activation (Figure 2d), as previously described (von Moltke et al., 2016; Schneider et al., 2018).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data and supported by citations.

claim: GATA3+ Th2 cells are important drivers of type two immunity during helminth infection.
source: GATA3+ Th2 cells, important drivers of type two immunity (Reynolds et al., 2012; Mohrs et al., 2005), were detected throughout all stages of infection, increased in frequency over time and showed high ki67 expression (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: GATA3+ Th2 cells were detected throughout all stages of H. polygyrus infection, increased in frequency over time and showed high ki67 expression.
source: GATA3+ Th2 cells, important drivers of type two immunity (Reynolds et al., 2012; Mohrs et al., 2005), were detected throughout all stages of infection, increased in frequency over time and showed high ki67 expression (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Ki67 expression strongly decreased at day 28 post infection for all cell types analyzed.
source: Interestingly, ki67 expression strongly decreased at day 28 post infection for all cell types analyzed (Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 4), which could be linked to the strong immunomodulatory properties reported during chronic worm infection (Maizels and McSorley, 2016; Grainger et al., 2010) (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2d and supplement 4.

claim: The decrease in ki67 expression at day 28 could be linked to strong immunomodulatory properties reported during chronic worm infection.
source: Interestingly, ki67 expression strongly decreased at day 28 post infection for all cell types analyzed (Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 4), which could be linked to the strong immunomodulatory properties reported during chronic worm infection (Maizels and McSorley, 2016; Grainger et al., 2010) (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citations to literature on chronic helminth immunomodulation.

claim: The frequencies of B220+, CD3+ CD4+, and CD64+ cells were highly comparable between confocal microscopy and spectral flow cytometry.
source: We observed that the frequencies of B220+, CD3+ CD4+, and CD64+ cells were highly comparable between confocal microscopy and spectral flow cytometry, while Siglec F+ cells were overrepresented in our spectral flow cytometry data and CD3+ CD4- cells were underrepresented.
evidence: This is stated as a result of comparing the two methods, with data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Siglec F+ cells were overrepresented in spectral flow cytometry data compared to confocal microscopy.
source: We observed that the frequencies of B220+, CD3+ CD4+, and CD64+ cells were highly comparable between confocal microscopy and spectral flow cytometry, while Siglec F+ cells were overrepresented in our spectral flow cytometry data and CD3+ CD4- cells were underrepresented.
evidence: This is stated as a result of comparing the two methods, with data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: CD3+ CD4- cells were underrepresented in spectral flow cytometry data compared to confocal microscopy.
source: We observed that the frequencies of B220+, CD3+ CD4+, and CD64+ cells were highly comparable between confocal microscopy and spectral flow cytometry, while Siglec F+ cells were overrepresented in our spectral flow cytometry data and CD3+ CD4- cells were underrepresented.
evidence: This is stated as a result of comparing the two methods, with data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Changes within immune cell populations at the peak of H. polygyrus infection were faithfully reported by both confocal microscopy and spectral flow cytometry.
source: However, changes within immune cell populations at the peak of H. polygyrus infection were faithfully reported by both confocal microscopy and spectral flow cytometry (Figure 2—figure supplement 5d), emphasizing that cell ratios defined by single cell analysis need to be carefully validated within the tissue before conclusions are drawn.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the two methods, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5d.

claim: Cell ratios defined by single cell analysis need to be carefully validated within the tissue before conclusions are drawn.
source: However, changes within immune cell populations at the peak of H. polygyrus infection were faithfully reported by both confocal microscopy and spectral flow cytometry (Figure 2—figure supplement 5d), emphasizing that cell ratios defined by single cell analysis need to be carefully validated within the tissue before conclusions are drawn.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation of differences in absolute frequencies between methods despite similar trends.

claim: Strong inflammatory immune responses observed during H. polygyrus development in the muscularis externa were specific to the infected tissue and were not observed to the same extent in the draining lymph nodes.
source: Another important conclusion from our analysis was that the strong inflammatory immune responses that we had observed during H. polygyrus development in the muscularis externa, were specific to the infected tissue and were not observed to the same extent in the draining lymph nodes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing lamina propria and lymph node data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: Ratios of ILC populations and T helper subsets were strikingly different between the lamina propria and the draining lymph nodes at steady state.
source: Furthermore, ratios of ILC populations and T helper subsets were also strikingly different between the lamina propria and the draining lymph nodes at steady state, as were their proliferation kinetics and changes in proportion throughout the course of H. polygyrus infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 6 and Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing data from the two tissues shown in the supplements.

claim: Proliferation kinetics and changes in proportion of ILC populations and T helper subsets throughout H. polygyrus infection were different between the lamina propria and draining lymph nodes.
source: Furthermore, ratios of ILC populations and T helper subsets were also strikingly different between the lamina propria and the draining lymph nodes at steady state, as were their proliferation kinetics and changes in proportion throughout the course of H. polygyrus infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 6 and Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing data from the two tissues shown in the supplements.

claim: RNA quality analysis using the Agilent TapeStation resulted in high RIN numbers (range 6.8–10 for naïve and 7.0–10 for day 14 H. polygyrus samples) from purified B cells, CD4 T cells and macrophages.
source: Our RNA quality analysis using the Agilent TapeStation resulted in high RIN numbers (range 6.8–10 for naïve and 7.0–10 for day 14 hr. polygyrus samples) (Figure 2—figure supplement 8e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA quality data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8e.

claim: No clear separation of the 18S and 28S peaks could be observed on the gel image or electropherograms from RNA extracted from intestinal immune cells.
source: However, no clear separation of the 18S and 28S peaks could be observed on the gel image or the electropherograms (Figure 2—figure supplement 8c,d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA quality data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8c,d.

claim: No RNA degradation was observed in naïve and day 14 H. polygyrus samples, suggesting that extraction of high-quality RNA is feasible using the cell isolation protocol.
source: While the RIN numbers might not have been correctly calculated, and a technical optimization of the TapeStation protocol might be necessary, no RNA degradation was observed in naïve and day 14 hr. polygyrus samples, suggesting that the extraction of high-quality RNA is feasible from both naïve and day 14 hr. polygyrus-infected mice using our cell isolation protocol.
evidence: This is concluded from the RNA quality analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: The cell isolation protocol and high-dimensional analysis characterized many known hallmarks of innate and adaptive anti-parasite immune responses throughout the entire course of helminth infection.
source: Thus, our cell isolation protocol and high-dimensional analysis allowed us to characterize many known hallmarks of innate and adaptive anti-parasite immune responses throughout the entire course of helminth infection.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion supported by all the flow cytometry and microscopy data presented.

claim: Changes in immune responses during helminth infection were validated using confocal microscopy.
source: We were able to validate these changes using confocal microscopy and while we could observe differences in the reported cell ratios, changes between naïve and infected samples were faithfully reported by both approaches.
evidence: This is stated as a validation approach, with data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Many immune response changes during helminth infection were only observed locally in the infected tissue, highlighting the requirement for good cell isolation techniques.
source: Importantly, many of these changes were only observed locally, highlighting the requirement for good cell isolation techniques to investigate intestinal responses against helminths directly.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing lamina propria and lymph node data.

claim: The optimized protocol has the potential to accelerate single-cell discoveries of local helminth immune responses through current single-cell analysis tools such as single cell RNA sequencing.
source: In addition to flow cytometric immunophenotyping, we were also able to extract high-quality RNA from cells isolated with our protocol, which could accelerate single-cell discoveries of local helminth immune responses through current single-cell analysis tools, such as single cell RNA sequencing, which has previously been unfeasible.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application, supported by the RNA quality data.

claim: Single cell RNA sequencing of local helminth immune responses has previously been unfeasible.
source: In addition to flow cytometric immunophenotyping, we were also able to extract high-quality RNA from cells isolated with our protocol, which could accelerate single-cell discoveries of local helminth immune responses through current single-cell analysis tools, such as single cell RNA sequencing, which has previously been unfeasible.
evidence: This is stated as context for the significance of the work, based on the technical challenges described.

source: For experimental infections, mice were infected with 200 L3 larvae by oral gavage at 6–8 weeks of age and intestines and draining lymph nodes were harvested at the indicated time points.
evidence: This describes the infection protocol used.

claim: Optimal digestion was achieved when intestinal segments were excised, cleaned, cut into small pieces, washed with 2 mM EDTA/HBSS three times for 10 min at 37°C with pulse vortexing, and digested in RPMI with 20% FBS, 1 mg/ml Collagenase A and 0.05 mg/ml DNAse for 30 min at 37°C.
source: Optimal digestion was achieved when intestinal segments were excised, cleaned and cut into small pieces. Samples were then washed with 2 mM EDTA/HBSS (Gibco) three times for 10 min at 37° C and 200 rpm in a shaking incubator, followed by three pulse vortexing steps at 2500 rpm (maximum speed) for 3 s after each incubation. After the final EDTA wash step, samples were digested in 10 ml RPMI (Gibco) containing 20% FBS (Gibco), 1 mg/ml Collagenase A (Roche #10103578001, 0.223 U/mg solid) and 0.05 mg/ml DNAse (Roche #10104159001, 2916 Kunitz units/mgL) for 30 min at 37°C and 200 rpm in a shaking incubator, with vigorous manual shaking every 5 min.
evidence: This describes the optimized protocol in detail.

claim: Duodenum draining mesenteric lymph nodes were identified as the most proximal lymph nodes of the mesenteric lymph node chain.
source: Individual duodenum draining mesenteric lymph nodes were identified as the most proximal lymph nodes of the mesenteric lymph node chain (Esterházy et al., 2019; Mayer et al., 2017), and were digested with 100 µg/mL Liberase TL and 100 µg/mL DNase I (both from Roche, Germany) for 30 min at 37°C and passed through a 70 µm cell strainer.
evidence: This describes the lymph node identification method, supported by citations.

claim: FlowSOM analysis was performed on 1,200,000 concatenated lamina propria cells with equal distribution of samples.
source: FlowSOM analysis was performed on 1,200,000 concatenated lamina propria and 1,000,000 concatenated lymph node cells, with an equal distribution of samples.
evidence: This describes the computational analysis approach.

claim: 121 clusters were identified as the most representative for both lamina propria and lymph node data sets in FlowSOM analysis.
source: Different cluster analyses were performed and 121 clusters were identified as the most representative for both data sets.
evidence: This describes the result of the FlowSOM clustering analysis.

claim: Experimental group sizes ranging from 3 to 5 animals were chosen to ensure that a two-fold difference between means could be detected with a power of at least 80%.
source: Experimental group sizes ranging from 3 to 5 animals were chosen to ensure that a two-fold difference between means could be detected with a power of at least 80%.
